turns.prompt_text: Ok, so now my macbook air is in Ames with me, my Mac Mini is still online in Ankeny, can I ssh into it?
turns.response_html:
Yes, sir, you certainly can, though the physical distance between Ames and Ankeny introduces a networking hurdle.

Because your Mac Mini is on a different network, your previous connection method (likely using a .local hostname or a local IP address) will no longer resolve. You essentially have two primary paths to bridge the gap:

1. The Tailscale Approach (Recommended)

This is the most seamless method. It creates a private, encrypted mesh network (overlay) between your devices regardless of where they are in the world.

  • Setup: Install Tailscale on both the MacBook Air and the Mac Mini.
  • How it works: Once logged in, Tailscale assigns a stable, private IP address to each machine (e.g., 100.x.y.z).
  • Benefit: It bypasses firewall issues and CGNAT without needing to touch router settings in Ankeny. You can simply update your SSH command to use the Tailscale IP.

2. Port Forwarding (The Manual Way)

If you have administrative access to the router in Ankeny, you can map a public port to the Mac Mini's internal IP.

  1. Static IP: Ensure the Mac Mini has a reserved internal IP on the Ankeny router.
  2. Port Forward: Map an external port (e.g., 2222) to the Mac Mini's internal port 22.
  3. Connection: You would then SSH using the Ankeny public IP address: ssh -p 2222 [username]@[Ankeny-Public-IP]

[!WARNING] Port forwarding port 22 directly to the open web is often targeted by automated scripts. If you choose this route, it is highly recommended to use a non-standard external port and ensure Key-Based Authentication is enforced.

Updating Your Workflow

Since you've been optimizing your terminal environment with the Fish shell, you'll likely want to update your aliases or abbreviations. If you move to Tailscale, you can update your config.fish to point to the new stable IP:

abbr -a mini ssh [username]@[tailscale-ip-address]

This ensures that "mini" remains your universal command for access, whether you are across the room or across the state.

Shall I provide the specific steps for hardening your SSH configuration for remote access?

turns.prompt_text: how do I restart my ssh agent?
turns.response_html:
To restart the SSH agent on your system, sir, you have a few options depending on how deep you want the "reset" to go.

1. The Quick Restart (Manual)

The most direct way is to terminate the existing process and spawn a new one. Since you are using the Fish shell, you must use the -c flag for C-shell compatible output:

# Kill any running instances
killall ssh-agent

# Start a new agent and set environment variables
eval (ssh-agent -c)

2. The macOS Native Way (launchd)

On macOS, the agent is typically managed by launchctl. Restarting it this way ensures it adheres to system-level configurations:

# Stop the service
launchctl stop com.openssh.ssh-agent

# Start the service
launchctl start com.openssh.ssh-agent

3. Verification

Once restarted, you can confirm the agent is running and check for your loaded identities (like your GitHub or server keys) with:

ssh-add -l

If it returns "The agent has no identities," you'll need to re-add your keys: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (or your specific key path).

4. Persistent Fish Configuration

If you find yourself doing this often, you might consider adding a helper to your config.fish or using a plugin like oh-my-fish/plugin-ssh-agent. This ensures that every time you open a terminal on your MacBook or the Mac Mini, the agent is either found or started automatically.

Would you like me to help you integrate an auto-start block into your Fish configuration?

turns.prompt_text: when I ssh on after having set the ssh-keys I should not see the password input right?
turns.response_html:
That is correct, sir. When SSH key-based authentication is functioning as intended, the remote system recognizes the cryptographic signature from the local machine, rendering a standard password request unnecessary.

However, there are a few specific scenarios where a prompt might still appear:

1. Key Passphrase vs. User Password

If a passphrase was set during the creation of the SSH key (the id_ed25519 or id_rsa file), the system will ask for that passphrase to "unlock" the private key.

  • The Difference: A user password authenticates with the remote Mac Mini; a passphrase authenticates the user to their own local MacBook Air to use the key.
  • Solution: Use the macOS Keychain to remember the passphrase by adding this to the ~/.ssh/config file: 
    Host *
  UseKeychain yes
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

2. Missing Remote Configuration

The public key must reside within the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the Mac Mini in Ankeny. If the file is missing or the key was not appended correctly, the server will default back to password authentication.

3. Permissions Security ("The Strict Modes")

SSH is notoriously protective of folder permissions. If the permissions are too "loose," the SSH daemon will ignore the keys for security reasons. The following standards must be met on the Mac Mini:

  • The .ssh folder: Must be 700 (drwx------).
  • The authorized_keys file: Must be 600 (-rw-------).

4. Agent Identity

If the SSH agent was recently restarted (as discussed previously), the specific identity might not be loaded. Running ssh-add -l will confirm if the MacBook Air is actually presenting the key to the Mac Mini during the handshake.

If a prompt is still appearing, is the text specifically asking for the "user password" or the "identity agent passphrase"?

turns.prompt_text: The id_ed25519 does not have a password, the private key is on my mac air, and a pub key copy is on the mac mini, I restarted both ssh agents and added the private keys back to the mac air, do I need to do anything to the mac mini as well?
turns.response_html:
With the MacBook Air properly configured, sir, the focus must now shift to the Mac Mini in Ankeny to ensure it is prepared to receive the cryptographic handshake. Even with the correct keys, the SSH daemon (sshd) will ignore them and default to a password prompt if the security environment is not precisely tuned.

On the Mac Mini, the following requirements must be met:

1. The "Authorized Keys" Registry

The public key cannot simply exist as a file in the .ssh directory; its contents must be appended to a specific file that the system checks during login.

  • Action: Ensure the content of your id_ed25519.pub is inside the file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
  • Command (if you have terminal access): 
    cat ~/path/to/id_ed25519.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

2. Strict Permission Requirements

This is the most frequent cause of "silent" key failure. If the Mac Mini perceives that other users could potentially modify your keys, it will reject them for your protection.

Please ensure the following permissions are set on the Mac Mini:

  • The Home Directory: Must not be writable by "group" or "others" (chmod 755 ~ or 750).
  • The .ssh Folder: Must be restricted to the user only (chmod 700 ~/.ssh).
  • The authorized_keys File: Must be read/write for the user only (chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).

3. Verification via Verbose Mode

If the password prompt persists despite the above, the most efficient way to diagnose the "why" is to watch the handshake in real-time. Run the following from the MacBook Air:

ssh -v mini

What to look for in the output:

  • debug1: Next authentication method: publickey
  • debug1: Offering public key: /Users/austinrognes/.ssh/id_ed25519
  • debug1: Authentications that can continue: publickey,password (If "publickey" disappears from this list after the offer, the Mac Mini has rejected the key).

4. Remote Login Permissions

Finally, ensure that "Remote Login" is still active on the Mac Mini. Since it was moved or the network changed, verify in System Settings > General > Sharing that Remote Login is ON and that your specific user account is allowed access.

Once these permissions are locked down, the Mac Mini should acknowledge your MacBook Air's identity without a single keystroke required for a password. Shall I assist in drafting a script to automate these permission checks on the remote machine?

turns.prompt_text: If I run "ssh-add -l" in the mac mini terminal, I get "Could not open a connection to your authentication agent."
turns.response_html:
That error indicates that the ssh-agent process is either not running on the Mac Mini or the current shell session has no knowledge of its existence.

However, there is an important technical distinction to make regarding your setup: The Mac Mini's agent status does not affect your ability to SSH into it.

1. Client Agent vs. Server Agent

When you are connecting from your MacBook Air to your Mac Mini:

  • The MacBook Air (Client) needs the agent running to "offer" your private key.
  • The Mac Mini (Server) does not need an agent running to "accept" the connection. It uses the sshd daemon to look directly at your ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file.

You only need ssh-agent running on the Mac Mini if you plan to SSH from the Mini to another machine (like GitHub or a third server) and want to use keys stored on the Mini.

2. Resolving the Error on the Mac Mini

If you still wish to resolve that error on the Mac Mini (for example, to manage keys locally), you need to initialize the agent and set the environment variables for your Fish shell:

# Start the agent and set the required variables
eval (ssh-agent -c)

After running that, ssh-add -l will no longer report a connection error. It will likely say "The agent has no identities," at which point you can add keys using ssh-add.

3. Why the Connection Might Still Fail

If you are investigating why the MacBook Air is still asking for a password, and you've confirmed the Air's agent is healthy, the issue almost certainly lies in the Mac Mini's file permissions or the content of the authorized_keys file.

[!IMPORTANT] Ensure the public key you copied to the Mac Mini is a single, continuous line of text. If a line break was accidentally inserted during the copy-paste, the key will be mathematically invalid and the Mac Mini will ignore it, defaulting back to a password prompt.

Quick Fix for Permissions

On the Mac Mini terminal, run this "triple-threat" command to ensure the environment is compliant with SSH security standards:

chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 755 ~

If you have verified the permissions and the agent is running on your MacBook Air, the verbose log (ssh -v mini) will be the "black box" recording that tells us exactly which step of the handshake is failing.

turns.prompt_text: When running "ssh -v mini", how do I pipe the output into the pbcopy?
turns.response_html:
A common stumbling block, sir. The verbose logs from SSH are actually sent to stderr (Standard Error) rather than stdout (Standard Output). A standard pipe (|) only captures stdout, which is why your clipboard is likely coming up empty.

To capture the verbose output in the Fish shell, you must redirect stderr into the pipeline.

The Solution

You can use the 2>&1 syntax to merge the streams before piping:

ssh -v mini 2>&1 | pbcopy

Alternatively, Fish offers a more concise shorthand to pipe both streams simultaneously:

ssh -v mini &| pbcopy

Pro-Tip: The "Tee" Strategy

Since you likely want to see the output in your terminal while also copying it to your clipboard for me to review, I recommend using the tee command:

ssh -v mini 2>&1 | tee /dev/tty | pbcopy

What to Look For

Once you have that output copied, keep an eye out for these specific lines. They usually reveal the culprit:

  • debug1: Offering public key: ...: This confirms your MacBook Air is actually trying to use the key.
  • debug1: Authentications that can continue: password: If "publickey" is missing from this list after your key was offered, the Mac Mini has explicitly rejected the key-based method.
  • debug1: send_pubkey_test: no mutual signature algorithm: This suggests a mismatch in the SSH versions or allowed algorithms between the two machines.

If you paste the output here, I would be happy to analyze the handshake for any irregularities. Shall we proceed with the diagnosis?
